It uses integer-scaled path weights and exhaustive enumeration, with no floating-point comparisons or external dependencies.

For all topologically ordered DAGs on at most 6 vertices having vertex 0 as sole source and at most 3 terminal sinks, and for Q<=3, enumerated every demand vector d_i/Q with max_i d_i=Q, every path-flow decomposition in multiples of 1/Q, and every candidate choice of one path per sink. No counterexample occurred among 43,404 feasible graph configurations, 5,448,556 decompositions, and 4,146,045 distinct aggregate flows.

final_writeup:
I do not obtain a proof or counterexample for the full conjecture. The strongest exact advance is a polynomial-time proof for every single-source instance with at most two sinks, including unequal demands. Exact solutions also follow when there is one sink, when b/d_max is integral, when the positive support has unique source-sink paths, and under an explicit local dominant-path certificate.

For the two-sink theorem, scale the demands to 1 and alpha<=1 and decompose x=f_1+f_2 into the two sink flows. The normalized sum g=f_1+f_2/alpha is a two-unit flow. Require an integral two-unit flow z to use every arc with x_a>1 at least once and every arc with x_a<alpha at most once. The fractional g satisfies these integer bounds: on x_a<alpha, g_a<=x_a/alpha<1, while everywhere g_a<=2. Integral lower/upper flow feasibility therefore supplies z. Its two unit paths, weighted 1 and alpha according to their sinks, meet the desired discrepancy by a three-case check according as z_a is 0, 1, or 2.

For general instances, grouping a polynomial path decomposition by ordered endpoint pair reduces the problem to choosing one path per group of weight at most d_max. Conditional-expectation rounding gives deterministic discrepancy at most min(B,sqrt((|V|-1)d_max B)), where B is total supply. Independent sampling and exact rejection checking improve this to sqrt(d_max B ceil(log_2(4|A|))/2) in expected polynomial time.

The remaining single-source frontier therefore requires at least three sinks with nonuniform demands. The abstract row-column obstruction recorded below shows that group weights alone cannot prove the conjecture; a full proof must exploit the switching and integrality structure of directed paths.

results.claim: Every rational input flow x has a polynomial-size rational source-to-sink path decomposition, whose total weight q_st for each ordered pair (s,t) satisfies q_st<=d_t<=d_max.
results.proof_sketch: Add a supersource with an arc of value b(s) into every source and a supersink with an arc of value d_t out of every sink. The resulting flow is conserved at all original vertices. Because the graph is acyclic, repeatedly subtract the minimum positive arc value on a supersource-to-supersink path; an arc becomes zero each time, so only polynomially many paths result. Stripping the added arcs gives the claimed decomposition. The weights ending at t sum to d_t, proving q_st<=d_t. All arithmetic consists of polynomially many operations on input rationals.

results.claim: After fixing the pair weights q_st, choosing one supported path P_st for every positive pair and assigning it weight q_st always produces a nonnegative unsplittable b-transshipment.
results.proof_sketch: Every selected path contributes +q_st at s, -q_st at t, and zero balance internally. The grouped decomposition has row sums b(s) and column sums d_t, so their sum has balance b. There is exactly one positive path for each selected ordered pair. If P_st is sampled with probability equal to its original path weight divided by q_st, then the resulting random arc flow Y also satisfies E[Y_a]=x_a for every arc.

results.claim: On rational inputs, any real feasible unsplittable solution can be replaced by one with polynomially bounded rational encoding; consequently, existence is in NP.
results.proof_sketch: Fix the at-most-one path used for each ordered pair in a real solution. Its path weights obey rational row and column equations, nonnegativity, and rational arc inequalities. This is a bounded rational polytope. A nonempty bounded rational polytope has a rational vertex; Cramer's rule and Hadamard's determinant bound give polynomial encoding length because there are at most |S+||S-| variables and all coefficients are 0 or 1. The paths and rational weights form a polynomial certificate verifiable by exact arithmetic.

results.claim: The facts q_st<=d_max and E[Y]=x are insufficient by themselves for arbitrary grouped incidence vectors.
results.proof_sketch: Set d_max=1 and take two unit-weight groups, each with three choices. Use coordinates a_ij for 1<=i,j<=3. Choice R_i of the first group contains the entire ith row, and choice C_j of the second contains the entire jth column. Under uniform fractional choices, x_ij=2/3. Every integral choice R_i,C_j gives y_ij=2 at their intersection, so the discrepancy is 4/3>1. This is not a graph counterexample; it proves that directed-path structure is essential.

results.claim: A dominant-path residual gives an exact, efficiently checkable sufficient condition for the target.
results.proof_sketch: For pair i, let q_i be its total weight, choose a maximum-weight supported path of weight f_i*, and put r_i=q_i-f_i*. Let C_i consist of arcs on which the supported paths of group i do not all agree. Outside C_i consolidation changes nothing. On an arc in C_i, the chosen group contribution differs from its fractional contribution by at most r_i: all weight other than f_i* totals r_i. Hence |y_a-x_a|<=sum_{i:a in C_i} r_i. If every such sum is at most d_max, the chosen paths solve the exact target.

results.claim: If every pair group has at most h supported paths and total supply B satisfies B<=h d_max/(h-1), the exact target holds; in particular, two-path groups suffice whenever B<=2d_max.
results.proof_sketch: A largest path in a group of at most h paths has weight at least q_i/h, so its residual is at most (1-1/h)q_i. The preceding residual bound is therefore at most sum_i r_i<=(1-1/h)B<=d_max on every arc. The construction and all comparisons are polynomial-time.

results.claim: There is a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm producing an unsplittable y with max_a |y_a-x_a|<=min(B,sqrt((|V|-1)d_max B)).
results.proof_sketch: Use the random supported-path choice from the second claim. Write p_ia for the probability that group i's path contains arc a and define Phi=sum_a(Y_a-x_a)^2. Independence gives E[Phi]=V:=sum_{a,i}q_i^2 p_ia(1-p_ia). Fix groups successively, each time choosing a supported path whose conditional expected Phi is no larger than the current conditional expectation. These are exact rational calculations, so the final Phi<=V. Moreover V<=sum_i q_i^2 sum_a p_ia<=sum_i d_max q_i(|V|-1)=(|V|-1)d_max B, since a DAG path has at most |V|-1 arcs. Each arc flow lies between 0 and B, also giving the bound B.

results.claim: An expected-polynomial-time exact sampler improves the general relaxed bound to max_a |y_a-x_a|<=sqrt(d_max B ceil(log_2(4|A|))/2).
results.proof_sketch: Choose the group paths independently. For a fixed arc, Hoeffding's inequality applies to independent variables with ranges q_i and sum_i q_i^2<=d_max B. With L=ceil(log_2(4|A|)) and lambda=sqrt(d_max B L/2), the probability that any arc has discrepancy exceeding lambda is at most 2|A|e^{-L}<=1/2. Sample until the exactly checkable inequalities 2(y_a-x_a)^2<=d_max B L all hold. Each trial uses exact rational sampling and verification, and the expected number of trials is at most two.

results.claim: If the positive-support digraph of x has at most one directed path for every ordered source-sink pair, then y=x is already unsplittable.
results.proof_sketch: Every path in the decomposition of x lies in its positive support. Under the hypothesis, all decomposition terms with the same endpoints use the identical path, so they can be combined into one weighted path without changing any arc value. Thus the discrepancy is zero. Uniqueness can be tested by dynamic programming in the DAG while capping path counts at two.

results.claim: The exact target holds in polynomial time whenever there is only one sink.
results.proof_sketch: Let B be total supply. Here B=d_max. Decompose x and, for each source, consolidate all its paths to the sole sink onto any one supported path with their total weight. This preserves b and gives at most one path per source-sink pair. Both x_a and the constructed y_a lie in [0,B] because each is a sum of source-to-sink path weights of total B. Therefore |y_a-x_a|<=B=d_max.

results.claim: Integral lower-and-upper flow feasibility lemma: if an integral-balance flow g lies between integral arc bounds l and u, an integral flow z with the same balances and bounds exists and is computable in polynomial time.
results.proof_sketch: Subtract l from every arc and adjust the integral vertex balances accordingly. Add a supersource and supersink in the standard way, with integral capacities u-l. The assumed g supplies a feasible fractional flow of the required value. Integral-capacity max-flow integrality supplies an integral flow of that value, and adding l back proves the lemma. Polynomial-time max-flow algorithms give the asserted running time.

results.claim: The exact target holds whenever b(v)/d_max is an integer for every vertex; this includes all single-source instances with equal sink demands.
results.proof_sketch: Put Delta=d_max and g=x/Delta. It has integral balances. Apply the integral-flow lemma with l_a=floor(g_a) and u_a=ceil(g_a), obtaining integral z, and set y=Delta z. Then |y_a-x_a|<Delta unless g_a is integral, in which case it is zero. Every sink has positive integral demand d_t/Delta<=1, hence exactly one unit. An integral path decomposition of the acyclic z therefore has exactly one unit path ending at each sink, so no ordered source-sink pair is repeated.

results.claim: For a single source and two sinks of scaled demands 1 and alpha<=1, there is a feasible integral two-unit flow z with lower bound 1 on H={a:x_a>1} and upper bound 1 on L={a:x_a<alpha}, with upper bound 2 elsewhere.
results.proof_sketch: Decompose the scaled x as f_1+f_2, where f_1 and f_2 have values 1 and alpha toward their respective sinks. Define g=f_1+f_2/alpha. This has integral balances +2 at the source and -1 at each sink. On H, g_a>=x_a>1. On L, since f_1,a+f_2,a=x_a<alpha, g_a=f_1,a+f_2,a/alpha<=x_a/alpha<1. Everywhere g_a<=2 because each normalized component is a unit path flow. Thus g satisfies the stated integral bounds, and the integral-flow lemma supplies z.

results.claim: The exact target is computable in polynomial time for every single-source instance with at most two sinks, with arbitrary rational demands.
results.proof_sketch: The one-sink case is already proved. With two sinks, decompose the integral z from the preceding claim into one unit path P_1 to the first sink and one unit path P_2 to the second. Route weights 1 and alpha on these paths. If z_a=0, the lower constraint gives x_a<=1, so the error is at most 1. If z_a=2, the upper constraint gives x_a>=alpha, while x_a<=1+alpha, so |1+alpha-x_a|<=1. If z_a=1, the routed value is either 1 or alpha; every x_a lies in [0,1+alpha], giving error at most 1 in either case. Rescaling by d_max proves the target. Decomposition, bounded integral flow, and rescaling are polynomial-time exact operations.

results.claim: No counterexample exists in the finite SSUF classes exhaustively checked by exhaust_ssuf.py.
results.proof_sketch: The checker enumerates every forward-arc graph mask, recursively lists every source-to-sink path, enumerates all weak compositions of each scaled demand among those paths, and then enumerates every choice of one path per sink. It checks the target as an integer inequality after scaling by Q. The runs found none among 4,146,045 distinct flows for n<=6, Q<=3, and none among 168,336 distinct flows for n<=5, Q<=5, always with at most three terminal sinks.
